function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact contents of the three new files that will be added to the repo:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image for the app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or GitHub Container Registry) whenever you push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) is a very small “Hello World” Node.js project.  
> The Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and CI workflow below are written with that minimal structure in mind.  
> If the repo contains additional files (e.g., a `package.json` with a different start script), tweak the commands accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is small yet fully functional.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (the default for many Node.js tutorials).  
> * Adjust the `CMD` line if your entry point is different (e.g., `npm start`).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` and inside it a file `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image repo
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`).  
> * If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Node.js App

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        # Uncomment and configure if you have a kubeconfig secret
        # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
        # with:
        #   manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
        #   images: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
        run: echo "Deploy step placeholder – configure as needed"
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username (or GitHub Container Registry username).  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token with `write:packages` scope.  
> * (Optional) `KUBECONFIG` – if you want the workflow to deploy automatically.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to the registry you configured.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow finishes, you can verify:

```bash
# List images in Docker Hub (replace USERNAME)
docker pull USERNAME/nodejs-welcome:latest
docker run -p 3000:3000 USERNAME/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` in a browser – you should see the “Hello World” response from the Node.js app.

---

That’s it! 🎉  
If you run into any hiccups (e.g., the app listens on a different port, or you need a different base image), just tweak the Dockerfile or the Kubernetes YAML accordingly. Happy coding!
